# Page: Model Architecture

# Model Architecture

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [scgpt/model/generation_model.py](scgpt/model/generation_model.py)
- [scgpt/model/model.py](scgpt/model/model.py)
- [scgpt/utils/util.py](scgpt/utils/util.py)

</details>



This page documents the core model architecture components of scGPT, focusing on `TransformerModel` and `TransformerGenerator` classes located in [scgpt/model/model.py]() and [scgpt/model/generation_model.py](). These transformer-based architectures provide the foundation for gene expression prediction, cell type classification, and perturbation prediction.

Related pages: See page 3.2 for tokenization via `GeneVocab`, page 3.3 for `Preprocessor` and `DataCollator`, page 3.4 for the training loop, and page 5 for `embed_data` function usage.

## Overview

scGPT implements two primary model classes in [scgpt/model/]():

1. **`TransformerModel`** [scgpt/model/model.py:28-500](): General-purpose foundation model for gene expression prediction, masked language modeling (MLM), cell type classification (CLS), masked value prediction for cell embedding (MVC), and domain adversarial regularization (DAR).

2. **`TransformerGenerator`** [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:25-350](): Specialized model for perturbation prediction tasks, using `AffineExprDecoder` to predict expression changes.

Both inherit from `nn.Module` and share similar encoder-transformer-decoder architectures but differ in their decoder components and training objectives.

**Architecture Diagram: Core Components and Data Flow**

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph Input["Input Tensors"]
        src["src: gene_ids<br/>[batch, seq_len]"]
        values["values: expression<br/>[batch, seq_len]"]
        mask["src_key_padding_mask<br/>[batch, seq_len]"]
        batch_labels["batch_labels<br/>[batch] (optional)"]
    end
    
    subgraph Encoders["Encoder Components"]
        GeneEncoder["GeneEncoder<br/>nn.Embedding + LayerNorm"]
        ContinuousValueEncoder["ContinuousValueEncoder<br/>2-layer MLP"]
        CategoryValueEncoder["CategoryValueEncoder<br/>nn.Embedding"]
        BatchLabelEncoder["BatchLabelEncoder<br/>nn.Embedding"]
        PertEncoder["nn.Embedding<br/>(TransformerGenerator only)"]
    end
    
    subgraph TransformerCore["Transformer Core"]
        TransformerEncoder["TransformerEncoder<br/>nlayers x (Self-Attn + FFN)"]
        FlashTransformerEncoder["FlashTransformerEncoderLayer<br/>(optional: FlashMHA)"]
        FastTransformerEncoder["FastTransformerEncoderWrapper<br/>(optional: Linear Attn)"]
    end
    
    subgraph Decoders["Decoder Components"]
        ExprDecoder["ExprDecoder<br/>3-layer MLP"]
        ClsDecoder["ClsDecoder<br/>nlayers_cls x Linear"]
        MVCDecoder["MVCDecoder<br/>inner product / concat query"]
        AffineExprDecoder["AffineExprDecoder<br/>coeff + bias (Generator)"]
        AdversarialDiscriminator["AdversarialDiscriminator<br/>(DAR objective)"]
    end
    
    subgraph Output["Output Tensors"]
        mlm_output["mlm_output<br/>[batch, seq_len]"]
        cell_emb["cell_emb<br/>[batch, d_model]"]
        cls_output["cls_output<br/>[batch, n_cls]"]
        mvc_output["mvc_output<br/>[batch, seq_len]"]
        dab_output["dab_output<br/>[batch, num_batches]"]
    end
    
    src --> GeneEncoder
    values --> ContinuousValueEncoder
    values --> CategoryValueEncoder
    batch_labels --> BatchLabelEncoder
    
    GeneEncoder --> TransformerEncoder
    ContinuousValueEncoder --> TransformerEncoder
    CategoryValueEncoder --> TransformerEncoder
    BatchLabelEncoder --> TransformerEncoder
    PertEncoder --> TransformerEncoder
    
    TransformerEncoder --> ExprDecoder
    TransformerEncoder --> ClsDecoder
    TransformerEncoder --> MVCDecoder
    TransformerEncoder --> AffineExprDecoder
    TransformerEncoder --> AdversarialDiscriminator
    
    ExprDecoder --> mlm_output
    ClsDecoder --> cls_output
    MVCDecoder --> mvc_output
    AffineExprDecoder --> mlm_output
    AdversarialDiscriminator --> dab_output
    TransformerEncoder --> cell_emb
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py:28-440](), [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:25-296]()

## Primary Model Classes

### TransformerModel

The `TransformerModel` class is the core architecture of scGPT, designed for modeling gene expression data and generating cell embeddings.

Key components and features:

- **Input**: Takes gene tokens, expression values, and optional batch labels
- **Encoding**: Combines gene embeddings with value embeddings
- **Transformer**: Processes the embeddings through multi-head attention layers
- **Cell Embedding**: Extracts cell-level representations from the transformer output
- **Decoding**: Multiple decoders for expression prediction, classification, and contrastive learning
- **Attention Options**: Supports both standard PyTorch transformers and optimized Flash Attention

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class TransformerModel {
        +__init__(ntoken, d_model, nhead, etc)
        +forward(src, values, src_key_padding_mask, etc)
        +generate(cell_emb, src, values, etc)
        +encode_batch(src, values, src_key_padding_mask, etc)
        -_encode(src, values, src_key_padding_mask, batch_labels)
        -_get_cell_emb_from_layer(layer_output, weights)
    }
    
    class GeneEncoder {
        +embedding
        +enc_norm
        +forward(x)
    }
    
    class ContinuousValueEncoder {
        +linear1
        +linear2
        +activation
        +forward(x)
    }
    
    class ExprDecoder {
        +fc
        +zero_logit
        +forward(x)
    }
    
    class ClsDecoder {
        +_decoder
        +out_layer
        +forward(x)
    }
    
    TransformerModel --> GeneEncoder
    TransformerModel --> ContinuousValueEncoder
    TransformerModel --> ExprDecoder
    TransformerModel --> ClsDecoder
    TransformerModel --> "TransformerEncoder"
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py:28-440]()

### TransformerGenerator

The `TransformerGenerator` is a specialized model architecture for perturbation prediction tasks, extending the base architecture with perturbation-specific components.

Key components and features:

- **Input**: Takes gene tokens, expression values, and perturbation flags
- **Encoding**: Combines gene embeddings, value embeddings, and perturbation embeddings
- **Transformer**: Processes the combined embeddings
- **Decoding**: Uses a specialized `AffineExprDecoder` for predicting perturbation effects
- **Prediction**: Supports specialized inference for perturbation prediction via `pred_perturb` method

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class TransformerGenerator {
        +__init__(ntoken, d_model, nhead, etc)
        +forward(src, values, input_pert_flags, etc)
        +pred_perturb(batch_data, include_zero_gene, etc)
        -_encode(src, values, input_pert_flags, src_key_padding_mask)
        -_get_cell_emb_from_layer(layer_output, weights)
    }
    
    class GeneEncoder {
        +embedding
        +enc_norm
        +forward(x)
    }
    
    class ContinuousValueEncoder {
        +linear1
        +linear2
        +activation
        +forward(x)
    }
    
    class PertEncoder {
        +embedding
        +forward(x)
    }
    
    class AffineExprDecoder {
        +coeff_decoder
        +bias_decoder
        +forward(x, values)
    }
    
    TransformerGenerator --> GeneEncoder
    TransformerGenerator --> ContinuousValueEncoder
    TransformerGenerator --> PertEncoder
    TransformerGenerator --> AffineExprDecoder
    TransformerGenerator --> "TransformerEncoder"
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:25-296]()

## Encoder Components

The encoder components transform gene tokens, expression values, batch labels, and perturbation flags into embeddings for the transformer layers.

### GeneEncoder

The `GeneEncoder` embeds gene tokens into continuous vector representations:

- Takes token IDs as input
- Uses an embedding layer followed by layer normalization
- Provides gene-specific embeddings for the transformer

```python
# GeneEncoder implementation
class GeneEncoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_embeddings, embedding_dim, padding_idx=None):
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(num_embeddings, embedding_dim, padding_idx=padding_idx)
        self.enc_norm = nn.LayerNorm(embedding_dim)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.embedding(x)  # (batch, seq_len, embsize)
        x = self.enc_norm(x)
        return x
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py:723-739](), [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:357-373]()

### Value Encoders

scGPT supports multiple types of value encoders to handle different types of expression data:

1. **ContinuousValueEncoder**: For continuous gene expression values
   - Projects scalar values to embedding space via neural network layers
   - Applies value clipping, ReLU activation, and layer normalization

2. **CategoryValueEncoder**: For categorical (binned) gene expression values
   - Embeds categorical values similar to the GeneEncoder
   - Useful when expression values are discretized

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Value Encoding"
        direction TB
        InputValues["Input Expression Values"]
        
        subgraph "ContinuousValueEncoder"
            CVC1["Linear Layer 1"]
            CVA["ReLU Activation"]
            CVC2["Linear Layer 2"]
            CVN["LayerNorm"]
        end
        
        subgraph "CategoryValueEncoder"
            CEM["Embedding Layer"]
            CEN["LayerNorm"]
        end
        
        InputValues --> IType{"Input Type?"}
        IType -->|"Continuous"| CVC1
        IType -->|"Categorical"| CEM
        
        CVC1 --> CVA --> CVC2 --> CVN
        CEM --> CEN
        
        CVN --> Embeddings["Value Embeddings"]
        CEN --> Embeddings
    end
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py:765-812]()

### PertEncoder

The `PertEncoder` in the `TransformerGenerator` model embeds perturbation flags:

- Takes perturbation flags (0 for control, 1 for perturbed, 2 for padding)
- Embeds them into continuous vector representations
- Helps the model understand which genes are perturbed in perturbation prediction tasks

Sources: [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:25-296]()

## Transformer Core

The transformer core consists of the multi-head attention layers that process the concatenated embeddings. scGPT provides multiple implementations:

### Standard Transformer

Uses PyTorch `TransformerEncoder` [scgpt/model/model.py:131-134]() with `TransformerEncoderLayer` [scgpt/model/model.py:131-132]().

### Flash Attention Transformer

Implemented via `FlashTransformerEncoderLayer` [scgpt/model/model.py:595-720](), using the `FlashMHA` class from `flash_attn.flash_attention` [scgpt/model/model.py:15-22]():

- Faster computation for long sequences
- Lower memory footprint
- Supports `pre_norm` and `post_norm` schemes [scgpt/model/model.py:633-661]()

### Linear Attention Transformer

Implemented via `FastTransformerEncoderWrapper` [scgpt/model/model.py:507-593](), using the `fast_transformers` library:

- Linear complexity attention mechanism
- Builds encoder via `TransformerEncoderBuilder` [scgpt/model/model.py:522-544]()
- Converts `src_key_padding_mask` to `LengthMask` [scgpt/model/model.py:547-563]()

**Transformer Core Configuration**

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| `use_fast_transformer` | Enable Flash or Linear attention | `False` |
| `fast_transformer_backend` | `"flash"` or `"linear"` | `"flash"` |
| `pre_norm` | Pre-normalization vs. post-normalization | `False` |
| `nhead` | Number of attention heads | - |
| `nlayers` | Number of transformer layers | - |
| `d_model` | Embedding dimension | - |
| `d_hid` | Feedforward hidden dimension | - |

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py:115-134](), [scgpt/model/model.py:507-720](), [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:88-107]()

## Decoder Components

The decoder components transform the transformer outputs into task-specific predictions.

### ExprDecoder

The `ExprDecoder` predicts gene expression values:

- Takes transformer outputs as input
- Applies multiple fully-connected layers with activations
- Optionally predicts zero probabilities for explicit zero modeling
- Returns predicted expression values

```python
# ExprDecoder simplified implementation
class ExprDecoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, explicit_zero_prob=False, use_batch_labels=False):
        super().__init__()
        d_in = d_model * 2 if use_batch_labels else d_model
        self.fc = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d_in, d_model),
            nn.LeakyReLU(),
            nn.Linear(d_model, d_model),
            nn.LeakyReLU(),
            nn.Linear(d_model, 1),
        )
        self.explicit_zero_prob = explicit_zero_prob
        if explicit_zero_prob:
            self.zero_logit = nn.Sequential(
                # Similar layers for zero probability prediction
            )
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py:848-888]()

### ClsDecoder

The `ClsDecoder` is used for cell type classification:

- Takes cell embeddings as input
- Applies multiple fully-connected layers with activations and layer normalization
- Returns class logits for cell type prediction

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py:890-918](), [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:521-549]()

### MVCDecoder

The `MVCDecoder` (Masked Value Prediction for Cell Embedding) predicts masked gene expression values from cell embeddings:

- Takes cell embeddings and gene embeddings as inputs
- Supports multiple architectural styles (inner product, concat query, sum query)
- Returns predicted expression values

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py:920-1011]()

### AffineExprDecoder

The `AffineExprDecoder` is a specialized decoder for perturbation prediction:

- Predicts gene expression changes in an affine form (Ax + b)
- Uses two separate decoders for coefficient (A) and bias (b) prediction
- Supports optional activation functions and adaptive bias
- Used in the `TransformerGenerator` model

```python
# AffineExprDecoder simplified implementation
class AffineExprDecoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, explicit_zero_prob=False, activation=None, 
                 tanh_coeff=False, adaptive_bias=False):
        super().__init__()
        self.explicit_zero_prob = explicit_zero_prob
        self.tanh_coeff = tanh_coeff
        self.adaptive_bias = adaptive_bias
        self.coeff_decoder = ExprDecoder(d_model, explicit_zero_prob=explicit_zero_prob)
        self.bias_decoder = ExprDecoder(d_model, explicit_zero_prob=explicit_zero_prob)
        
        self.activation = activation
        if activation is not None:
            self.activation = getattr(nn, activation)()
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:376-442]()

## Model Forward Pass and Tasks

The model architecture supports several tasks through different forward pass operations:

### Main Forward Pass

The main forward pass in both `TransformerModel` and `TransformerGenerator` follows these steps:

1. Encode gene tokens, expression values, and optional batch labels/perturbation flags
2. Process the embeddings through the transformer encoder
3. Extract cell embeddings from the transformer output
4. Decode the transformer output for various tasks

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Input as "Input Data"
    participant Encoders as "Encoder Components"
    participant Transformer as "Transformer Encoder"
    participant Decoders as "Decoder Components"
    participant Output as "Task Outputs"
    
    Input->>Encoders: gene tokens, values, masks
    Note over Encoders: GeneEncoder, ValueEncoder, etc.
    Encoders->>Transformer: combined embeddings
    Note over Transformer: Self-attention + FFN layers
    Transformer->>Decoders: contextualized embeddings
    Note over Decoders: ExprDecoder, ClsDecoder, etc.
    Decoders->>Output: predictions, embeddings
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py:314-440](), [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:175-262]()

### Supported Tasks

The architecture supports various tasks through different components:

1. **Gene Expression Prediction**: Using the `ExprDecoder` or `AffineExprDecoder`
2. **Cell Type Classification**: Using the `ClsDecoder`
3. **Contrastive Cell Embedding (CCE)**: Uses cosine similarity between cell embeddings
4. **Masked Value Prediction (MVC)**: Using the `MVCDecoder`
5. **Elastic Cell Similarity (ECS)**: Optimizes cell embeddings to maintain similarity structure
6. **Perturbation Prediction**: Specialized in `TransformerGenerator` via `pred_perturb`

## Generation and Inference

The model architecture includes specialized methods for generation and inference:

### TransformerModel.generate

The `generate` method [scgpt/model/model.py:234-312]() generates gene expression values conditioned on a cell embedding:

**Signature:**
```python
def generate(
    self,
    cell_emb: Tensor,  # (batch, embsize)
    src: Tensor,       # (batch, seq_len)
    values: Optional[Tensor] = None,
    src_key_padding_mask: Optional[Tensor] = None,
    gen_iters: int = 1,
    batch_labels: Optional[Tensor] = None,
) -> Tensor
```

**Steps:**
1. Encode gene tokens and values via `self.encoder` and `self.value_encoder` [scgpt/model/model.py:266-276]()
2. Replace first token embedding with `cell_emb` [scgpt/model/model.py:286]()
3. Apply domain-specific batch normalization if enabled [scgpt/model/model.py:278-284]()
4. Run `self.transformer_encoder` forward pass [scgpt/model/model.py:292-294]()
5. Decode via `self.decoder` to get predicted expression [scgpt/model/model.py:298-310]()

### TransformerGenerator.pred_perturb

The `pred_perturb` method [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:295-349]() predicts perturbed gene expression:

**Signature:**
```python
def pred_perturb(
    self,
    batch_data,
    include_zero_gene="batch-wise",  # "all" or "batch-wise"
    gene_ids=None,
    amp=True,
) -> Tensor
```

**Steps:**
1. Extract `ori_gene_values` and `pert_flags` from `batch_data.x` [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:313-315]()
2. Select input gene IDs based on `include_zero_gene` strategy [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:318-324]()
3. Map raw IDs to vocab IDs via `map_raw_id_to_vocab_id` [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:328-329]()
4. Forward pass with `input_pert_flags` [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:335-345]()
5. Return predicted expression values [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:346-348]()

### encode_batch

Both models provide `encode_batch` [scgpt/model/model.py:442-499](), [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:264-293]() for batch processing:

**Key Parameters:**
- `batch_size`: Sub-batch size for memory management
- `output_to_cpu`: Move outputs to CPU to save GPU memory
- `time_step`: Extract specific time step (e.g., CLS token at position 0)
- `return_np`: Return numpy array instead of torch tensor

**Usage:**
```python
# Process large dataset in manageable batches
outputs = model.encode_batch(
    src=src_tensor,
    values=values_tensor,
    src_key_padding_mask=mask_tensor,
    batch_size=64,
    batch_labels=batch_labels,
    output_to_cpu=True,
    time_step=0,  # Extract CLS token only
)
```

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py:234-313](), [scgpt/model/model.py:442-499](), [scgpt/model/generation_model.py:264-349]()

## Integration with Data Processing

The model architecture integrates with the data processing pipeline (see page 3.3):

**Input Preparation:**
- Gene names tokenized via `GeneVocab` [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py]() → `src` tensor (page 3.2)
- Expression values preprocessed by `Preprocessor` → `values` tensor (page 3.3)
- `DataCollator` creates `src_key_padding_mask` for variable-length sequences (page 3.3)
- Batch labels encoded as integers for domain-specific batch normalization

**Pipeline Flow:**
```
AnnData → Preprocessor → GeneVocab → DataCollator → TransformerModel → embed_data
```

**Key Configuration Parameters:**

| Parameter | Purpose | Options |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `input_emb_style` | How to combine gene + value embeddings | `"continuous"`, `"category"`, `"scaling"` |
| `n_input_bins` | Number of bins for categorical encoding | Integer (e.g., 51) |
| `cell_emb_style` | How to extract cell embedding from sequence | `"cls"`, `"avg-pool"`, `"w-pool"` |
| `use_batch_labels` | Enable batch-aware encoding | Boolean |
| `domain_spec_batchnorm` | Domain-specific batch normalization | `False`, `True`, `"dsbn"`, `"batchnorm"` |

For tokenization details, see page 3.2. For data collation, see page 3.3. For training objectives, see page 3.4.

Sources: [scgpt/model/model.py:29-56](), [scgpt/model/model.py:64-74]()

## Summary

The scGPT model architecture consists of two main transformer-based models:

1. `TransformerModel`: The core architecture for general single-cell data tasks
2. `TransformerGenerator`: A specialized architecture for perturbation prediction

Both models combine gene embeddings with expression value embeddings (and optionally batch or perturbation embeddings), process them through transformer layers, and decode the outputs for various tasks including expression prediction, cell type classification, and perturbation prediction.

The architecture is modular with specialized encoders and decoders for different input types and tasks, making it adaptable to various single-cell genomics applications.

---

# Page: Tokenization and Vocabulary

# Tokenization and Vocabulary

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [poetry.lock](poetry.lock)
- [scgpt/preprocess.py](scgpt/preprocess.py)
- [scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py](scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py)
- [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py](scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This page documents the tokenization and vocabulary management systems in scGPT. These components handle the conversion of gene expression data into tokenized sequences suitable for transformer model input. For information about data preprocessing before tokenization, see [Data Processing Pipeline](#3.3). For model-level embedding after tokenization, see [Cell Embedding System](#5).

---

## Overview

scGPT's tokenization system converts single-cell gene expression matrices into sequences of gene tokens paired with expression values. The vocabulary maps gene names (symbols or IDs) to integer indices that the transformer can process. Unlike traditional NLP tokenization, scGPT's tokenizer operates on gene-level granularity where each gene is a discrete token.

**Sources:** [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:1-474]()

---

## GeneVocab Class

### Class Structure

The `GeneVocab` class extends `torchtext.vocab.Vocab` to provide gene-specific vocabulary management with support for special tokens and default values.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "GeneVocab Class"
        GV[GeneVocab]
        TTV[torchtext.vocab.Vocab]
        
        GV -->|extends| TTV
        
        subgraph "Construction Methods"
            INIT["__init__(gene_list_or_vocab)"]
            FROM_FILE["from_file(file_path)"]
            FROM_DICT["from_dict(token2idx)"]
        end
        
        subgraph "Core Properties"
            VOCAB_DICT["vocab: OrderedDict"]
            DEFAULT_IDX["default_index: int"]
            PAD_TOKEN["pad_token: str"]
        end
        
        subgraph "Key Methods"
            GET_ITEM["__getitem__(token) -> int"]
            CONTAINS["__contains__(token) -> bool"]
            SET_DEFAULT["set_default_token(token)"]
            SAVE_JSON["save_json(file_path)"]
            INSERT["insert_token(token, idx)"]
        end
        
        GV --> INIT
        GV --> FROM_FILE
        GV --> FROM_DICT
        
        GV --> VOCAB_DICT
        GV --> DEFAULT_IDX
        GV --> PAD_TOKEN
        
        GV --> GET_ITEM
        GV --> CONTAINS
        GV --> SET_DEFAULT
        GV --> SAVE_JSON
        GV --> INSERT
    end
```

**Sources:** [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:20-197]()

### Initialization and Loading

The `GeneVocab` can be created in three ways:

| Method | Input | Use Case |
|--------|-------|----------|
| `__init__` | List of gene names or existing Vocab | Creating new vocabulary from scratch |
| `from_file` | Path to .pkl or .json file | Loading pretrained vocabularies |
| `from_dict` | Dictionary mapping tokens to indices | Converting from external formats |

**Key Parameters:**
- `specials`: List of special tokens (e.g., `["<pad>", "<cls>", "<eoc>"]`)
- `special_first`: Whether to place special tokens at beginning of vocabulary
- `default_token`: Token to return for out-of-vocabulary queries (typically `"<pad>"`)

**Sources:** [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:25-109]()

### Vocabulary Construction Flow

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START["Input: Gene Names or File Path"]
    
    subgraph "Loading Methods"
        FROM_LIST["from gene_list: List[str]"]
        FROM_FILE_JSON["from vocab.json"]
        FROM_FILE_PKL["from vocab.pkl"]
        FROM_DICT_MAP["from token2idx dict"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Internal Processing"
        BUILD_VOCAB["_build_vocab_from_iterator()"]
        COUNTER["Counter: count frequencies"]
        ORDERED_DICT["OrderedDict: sorted tokens"]
        ADD_SPECIALS["Add special tokens"]
        TORCH_VOCAB["torch_vocab.vocab()"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Final Vocabulary"
        GENEVOCAB["GeneVocab instance"]
        TOKEN_MAP["token -> idx mapping"]
        DEFAULT_SET["default_index set"]
        PAD_SET["pad_token set"]
    end
    
    START --> FROM_LIST
    START --> FROM_FILE_JSON
    START --> FROM_FILE_PKL
    START --> FROM_DICT_MAP
    
    FROM_LIST --> BUILD_VOCAB
    BUILD_VOCAB --> COUNTER
    COUNTER --> ORDERED_DICT
    ORDERED_DICT --> ADD_SPECIALS
    ADD_SPECIALS --> TORCH_VOCAB
    
    FROM_FILE_JSON --> FROM_DICT_MAP
    FROM_FILE_PKL --> GENEVOCAB
    FROM_DICT_MAP --> GENEVOCAB
    TORCH_VOCAB --> GENEVOCAB
    
    GENEVOCAB --> TOKEN_MAP
    GENEVOCAB --> DEFAULT_SET
    GENEVOCAB --> PAD_SET
    
    TOKEN_MAP --> OUTPUT["vocab['gene_name'] -> int"]
```

**Sources:** [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:66-155]()

---

## Special Tokens

scGPT uses three primary special tokens for sequence structuring:

| Token | Purpose | Position | Model Configs Key |
|-------|---------|----------|------------------|
| `<pad>` | Padding sequences to uniform length | Throughout sequence | `pad_token` |
| `<cls>` | Classification/cell representation | Beginning of sequence | Used in `append_cls` |
| `<eoc>` | End of cell marker | End of sequence | Listed in specials |

### Special Token Usage Pattern

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Data as "Raw Gene Matrix"
    participant Tokenize as "tokenize_batch()"
    participant Vocab as "GeneVocab"
    participant Output as "Token Sequence"
    
    Data->>Tokenize: counts [n_genes]
    Tokenize->>Tokenize: Extract nonzero genes
    
    alt append_cls=True
        Tokenize->>Vocab: Get cls_id = vocab["<cls>"]
        Tokenize->>Output: Insert (cls_id, 0) at position 0
    end
    
    loop For each nonzero gene
        Tokenize->>Vocab: gene_name -> gene_id
        Tokenize->>Output: Append (gene_id, expression)
    end
    
    Note over Output: Result: [(cls, 0), (gene1, expr1), ...]
```

The `<cls>` token's embedding at position 0 is extracted as the cell-level representation during inference, similar to BERT's approach.

**Sources:** [scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py:78-90](), [scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py:136-137](), [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:205-211]()

---

## Tokenization Process

### Core Tokenization Functions

The tokenization pipeline transforms dense count matrices into sparse token sequences:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Input Data"
        COUNT_MAT["Count Matrix<br/>[batch_size, n_genes]"]
        GENE_IDS["Gene IDs<br/>[n_genes]"]
        VOCAB["GeneVocab"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Tokenization Steps"
        TOKENIZE["tokenize_batch()"]
        PAD["pad_batch()"]
        MASK["random_mask_value()<br/>(optional)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Format"
        TOKEN_SEQ["Token Sequences<br/>genes: [batch, max_len]<br/>values: [batch, max_len]"]
    end
    
    COUNT_MAT --> TOKENIZE
    GENE_IDS --> TOKENIZE
    VOCAB --> TOKENIZE
    
    TOKENIZE --> PAD
    VOCAB --> PAD
    PAD --> MASK
    MASK --> TOKEN_SEQ
```

**Sources:** [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:249-474]()

### tokenize_batch Function

Converts raw expression data to token pairs `(gene_id, expression_value)`:

**Function Signature:**
```python
tokenize_batch(
    data: np.ndarray,              # [batch_size, n_genes]
    gene_ids: np.ndarray,          # [n_genes]
    return_pt: bool = True,
    append_cls: bool = True,
    include_zero_gene: bool = False,
    cls_id: int = "<cls>",
    mod_type: np.ndarray = None,   # For multi-omics
) -> List[Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]]
```

**Algorithm:**
1. For each cell (row) in the batch:
   - Extract non-zero gene indices (unless `include_zero_gene=True`)
   - Retrieve corresponding gene IDs and expression values
   - If `append_cls=True`: Insert `(cls_id, 0)` at position 0
   - Convert to PyTorch tensors if `return_pt=True`

**Output:** List of tuples `(genes, values, mod_types)` per cell

**Sources:** [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:249-309]()

### pad_batch Function

Ensures uniform sequence length across batch via padding or sampling:

**Function Signature:**
```python
pad_batch(
    batch: List[Tuple],
    max_len: int,
    vocab: Vocab,
    pad_token: str = "<pad>",
    pad_value: int = 0,
    cls_appended: bool = True,
    vocab_mod: Vocab = None,
) -> Dict[str, torch.Tensor]
```

**Padding Strategy:**

| Scenario | Action |
|----------|--------|
| `len(genes) > max_len` | Random sample `max_len` genes (preserving `<cls>` if present) |
| `len(genes) < max_len` | Append `pad_token` IDs and `pad_value` expressions |
| `len(genes) == max_len` | No modification |

**Output:**
```python
{
    "genes": torch.Tensor,      # [batch_size, max_len]
    "values": torch.Tensor,     # [batch_size, max_len]
    "mod_types": torch.Tensor,  # [batch_size, max_len] (optional)
}
```

**Sources:** [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:312-396]()

### Combined Pipeline Function

The `tokenize_and_pad_batch()` function provides a single-call interface:

```python
tokenize_and_pad_batch(
    data: np.ndarray,
    gene_ids: np.ndarray,
    max_len: int,
    vocab: Vocab,
    pad_token: str,
    pad_value: int,
    append_cls: bool = True,
    include_zero_gene: bool = False,
    cls_token: str = "<cls>",
) -> Dict[str, torch.Tensor]
```

This is the standard entry point used by the DataCollator for batch preparation.

**Sources:** [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:399-439]()

---

## Expression Value Binning

While tokenization handles gene identity, expression values can be discretized into bins before being fed to the model. This binning occurs in the preprocessing stage.

### Binning Process

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Input"
        RAW["Raw Counts<br/>continuous values"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Preprocessing (Preprocessor)"
        NORM["Normalize total counts"]
        LOG["Log1p transform"]
        BIN_START["binning=n_bins parameter"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Binning Algorithm"
        NONZERO["Extract non-zero values"]
        QUANTILE["Compute quantiles<br/>np.linspace(0, 1, n_bins-1)"]
        DIGITIZE["_digitize() with bins"]
        ASSIGN["Assign bin indices 1 to n_bins-1"]
        ZERO["Keep zeros as bin 0"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output"
        BINNED["Binned Values<br/>X_binned layer"]
        EDGES["Bin Edges<br/>obsm['bin_edges']"]
    end
    
    RAW --> NORM
    NORM --> LOG
    LOG --> BIN_START
    
    BIN_START --> NONZERO
    NONZERO --> QUANTILE
    QUANTILE --> DIGITIZE
    DIGITIZE --> ASSIGN
    ZERO --> BINNED
    ASSIGN --> BINNED
    QUANTILE --> EDGES
```

**Key Implementation Details:**

- **Bin 0 reserved for zeros:** Ensures zero values are explicitly represented
- **Per-cell quantiles:** Each cell's non-zero values determine bin boundaries independently
- **Uniform distribution:** `np.quantile()` with `np.linspace(0, 1, n_bins-1)` creates equal-probability bins
- **Randomized assignment:** `_digitize()` with `side="both"` spreads values uniformly when bin edges overlap

**Configuration:** Default `n_bins=51` in most tutorials (50 expression bins + 1 zero bin)

**Sources:** [scgpt/preprocess.py:172-211](), [scgpt/preprocess.py:239-271](), [scgpt/preprocess.py:274-303]()

---

## Integration with Data Pipeline

### Vocabulary in embed_data Workflow

The following diagram shows how `GeneVocab` integrates with the inference pipeline:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Model Directory"
        VOCAB_FILE["vocab.json"]
        MODEL_FILE["best_model.pt"]
        CONFIG_FILE["args.json"]
    end
    
    subgraph "embed_data() Function"
        LOAD_VOCAB["GeneVocab.from_file(vocab.json)"]
        ADD_SPEC["Add special tokens if missing"]
        MAP_GENES["Map adata.var[gene_col] to vocab IDs"]
        FILTER["Filter unmapped genes"]
        ID_IN_VOCAB["adata.var['id_in_vocab']"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Tokenization"
        DATASET["Dataset.__getitem__()"]
        COLLATOR["DataCollator"]
        BATCH["Padded Batches"]
    end
    
    VOCAB_FILE --> LOAD_VOCAB
    LOAD_VOCAB --> ADD_SPEC
    ADD_SPEC --> MAP_GENES
    MAP_GENES --> FILTER
    FILTER --> ID_IN_VOCAB
    
    ID_IN_VOCAB --> DATASET
    DATASET --> COLLATOR
    COLLATOR --> BATCH
```

**Matching Process:**
1. Load vocabulary from model directory
2. For each gene in `adata.var[gene_col]`:
   - Check if `gene in vocab`
   - Assign `vocab[gene]` to `adata.var["id_in_vocab"]`
   - Assign `-1` if gene not in vocabulary
3. Filter to genes with `id_in_vocab >= 0`
4. Log matching statistics

**Sources:** [scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py:207-220]()

### DataCollator Usage

The `DataCollator` class (documented in [Data Processing Pipeline](#3.3)) calls tokenization functions to prepare batches:

```python
# Inside DataCollator.__call__()
batch = tokenize_and_pad_batch(
    data=data,
    gene_ids=gene_ids,
    max_len=self.max_length,
    vocab=self.vocab,
    pad_token=self.pad_token_id,
    pad_value=self.pad_value,
)
```

The collator also handles:
- Masked language modeling (MLM) token masking
- Binning of expression values
- Sampling sequences that exceed `max_length`

**Sources:** [scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py:96-114]()

---

## Masking for Training

### random_mask_value Function

During training, a subset of expression values can be masked to train masked language models:

```python
random_mask_value(
    values: torch.Tensor,
    mask_ratio: float = 0.15,
    mask_value: int = -1,
    pad_value: int = 0,
) -> torch.Tensor
```

**Masking Strategy:**
1. Identify non-padding positions (`value != pad_value`)
2. Randomly select `mask_ratio` × `n_non_padding` positions
3. Replace selected values with `mask_value` (typically `-1`)
4. Keep gene IDs unchanged (only mask expression values)

This differs from BERT-style masking where the token IDs themselves are masked. In scGPT, gene identities remain visible while their expression levels are hidden.

**Sources:** [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:442-473]()

---

## Practical Usage Examples

### Creating a Vocabulary from Gene List

```python
from scgpt.tokenizer import GeneVocab

# Define gene list and special tokens
gene_names = ["CD3D", "CD4", "CD8A", "CD19", "MS4A1"]
specials = ["<pad>", "<cls>", "<eoc>"]

# Create vocabulary
vocab = GeneVocab(
    gene_list_or_vocab=gene_names,
    specials=specials,
    special_first=True,
    default_token="<pad>",
)

# Token lookup
gene_id = vocab["CD3D"]  # Returns: 3 (after 3 special tokens)
vocab.set_default_index(vocab["<pad>"])  # Out-of-vocab queries return pad_id
```

### Loading Pretrained Vocabulary

```python
from pathlib import Path
from scgpt.tokenizer import GeneVocab

model_dir = Path("/path/to/model")
vocab = GeneVocab.from_file(model_dir / "vocab.json")

# Check vocabulary size
print(f"Vocabulary size: {len(vocab)}")

# Verify special tokens
assert "<pad>" in vocab
assert "<cls>" in vocab
```

### Tokenizing a Single Cell

```python
import numpy as np
import torch
from scgpt.tokenizer import tokenize_batch

# Raw data
counts = np.array([[0, 5.2, 0, 3.1, 0, 8.7]])  # 1 cell, 6 genes
gene_ids = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5])  # vocab indices
cls_id = vocab["<cls>"]

# Tokenize
tokenized = tokenize_batch(
    data=counts,
    gene_ids=gene_ids,
    append_cls=True,
    cls_id=cls_id,
    include_zero_gene=False,  # Only keep expressed genes
)

# Result: [(genes, values, None)]
genes, values, _ = tokenized[0]
# genes:  tensor([cls_id, 1, 3, 5])
# values: tensor([0., 5.2, 3.1, 8.7])
```

### End-to-End Batch Preparation

```python
from scgpt.tokenizer import tokenize_and_pad_batch

# Prepare batch
batch_dict = tokenize_and_pad_batch(
    data=counts,
    gene_ids=gene_ids,
    max_len=1200,
    vocab=vocab,
    pad_token="<pad>",
    pad_value=0,
    append_cls=True,
    cls_token="<cls>",
)

# Output structure
# batch_dict["genes"]:  [batch_size, max_len]  (gene token IDs)
# batch_dict["values"]: [batch_size, max_len]  (expression values)
```

**Sources:** [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:20-474]()

## Summary Table

| Component | Location | Purpose |
|-----------|----------|---------|
| `GeneVocab` | [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:20-197]() | Core vocabulary class, maps gene names to indices |
| `tokenize_batch` | [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:249-309]() | Converts count matrices to token sequences |
| `pad_batch` | [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py:312-396]() | Pads/samples sequences to uniform length |

The tokenization system provides the critical bridge between raw single-cell count matrices and the transformer model's input requirements, handling gene vocabulary management, sequence formatting, and expression value discretization.

# Page: Data Processing Pipeline

# Data Processing

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)
- [poetry.lock](poetry.lock)
- [scgpt/data_collator.py](scgpt/data_collator.py)
- [scgpt/preprocess.py](scgpt/preprocess.py)
- [scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py](scgpt/tasks/cell_emb.py)
- [scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py](scgpt/tokenizer/gene_tokenizer.py)

</details>



This document explains the data processing pipeline in scGPT, covering how single-cell RNA-seq data is preprocessed, tokenized, and collated before being fed to the model. For information about the model architecture itself, see [Model Architecture](#2.1), and for details on the training process, see [Training System](#2.3).

## Overview

Data processing in scGPT transforms raw gene expression matrices into a format suitable for transformer-based model training. The pipeline consists of several key steps that prepare single-cell data for the model.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Raw["Raw Gene Expression Data"] --> Preprocessing["Preprocessing Steps"]
    Preprocessing --> Tokenization["Gene Tokenization"]
    Tokenization --> Collation["Data Collation"]
    Collation --> ModelInput["Model-Ready Data"]
    
    subgraph "Preprocessing Pipeline"
        P1["Filter Genes"]
        P2["Normalize Counts"]
        P3["Log Transform"]
        P4["Select HVGs"]
        P5["Bin Expression Values"]
        
        P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5
    end
    
    Preprocessing -.-> "Preprocessing Pipeline"
```

**Data Processing Pipeline Overview**

Sources: [scgpt/data_collator.py]()

## Preprocessing Steps

Before feeding data into the scGPT model, several preprocessing steps are applied to the raw gene expression data:

1. **Filtering**: Removing low-quality cells and genes with low expression
2. **Normalization**: Scaling gene counts to account for sequencing depth differences
3. **Log Transformation**: Applying log(1+x) transformation to compress the dynamic range
4. **HVG Selection**: Selecting highly variable genes to focus on the most informative features
5. **Binning**: Discretizing continuous expression values into bins

The binning step is particularly important as it transforms continuous expression values into a discrete set of "tokens" that can be processed by the transformer model.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    ExprValues["Continuous Expression Values"] --> Binning["Binning Function"]
    Binning --> DiscValues["Discretized Values (0-50)"]
    
    subgraph "Expression Value Binning"
        BinFunc["binning(row, n_bins=51)"]
    end
    
    Binning -.-> "Expression Value Binning"
```

**Expression Value Binning Process**

Sources: [scgpt/data_collator.py:87-91]()

## Data Collation with DataCollator

The `DataCollator` class is responsible for preparing batches of data for model training. It handles tokenization, padding, and masking operations.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class DataCollator {
        +do_padding: bool
        +pad_token_id: int
        +pad_value: int
        +do_mlm: bool
        +do_binning: bool
        +mlm_probability: float
        +mask_value: int
        +max_length: int
        +sampling: bool
        +keep_first_n_tokens: int
        +__call__(examples): Dict
        -_mask(expressions): Tensor
        -_sample_or_truncate_plus_pad(genes, expressions, max_length): Tuple
        -_sample(genes, expressions, max_length): Tuple
        -_pad(genes, expressions, max_length): Tuple
    }
```

**DataCollator Class Structure**

Sources: [scgpt/data_collator.py:10-202]()

### Key Features of DataCollator

1. **Padding**: Ensures all sequences in a batch have the same length by padding shorter sequences
2. **Masking**: Implements Masked Language Modeling (MLM) strategy by randomly masking expression values
3. **Sampling/Truncation**: Handles sequences longer than the maximum length by either sampling or truncation
4. **Binning**: Converts continuous expression values to discrete bins

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["Input Batch"] --> MaxLength["Determine Max Length"]
    MaxLength --> Binning["Apply Binning (Optional)"]
    Binning --> SampleTruncPad["Sample/Truncate and Pad"]
    SampleTruncPad --> Stack["Stack Tensors"]
    Stack --> Masking["Apply Masking (Optional)"]
    Masking --> Output["Output Batch Dictionary"]
    
    subgraph "DataCollator.__call__ Flow"
        Process["Process each example:\n- Bin expressions\n- Sample/truncate if too long\n- Pad if too short"]
    end
    
    Binning -.-> "DataCollator.__call__ Flow"
```

**DataCollator Processing Flow**

Sources: [scgpt/data_collator.py:64-113]()

## Masking for Masked Value Learning

The masking process is a critical part of scGPT's training strategy, enabling the model to learn from partially obscured data:

1. A probability matrix determines which positions to mask
2. Padding positions and special token positions (first n tokens) are excluded from masking
3. Random positions are masked according to the specified probability
4. Masked positions are filled with a special mask value (-1 by default)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Expr["Expression Values"] --> ProbMatrix["Create Probability Matrix"]
    ProbMatrix --> Exclude["Exclude Padding & Special Tokens"]
    Exclude --> SampleMask["Sample Mask Positions"]
    SampleMask --> Replace["Replace with Mask Value"]
    Replace --> MaskedExpr["Masked Expressions"]
    
    subgraph "Masking Process"
        M1["probability_matrix = full(shape, mlm_probability)"]
        M2["Set 0 probability for pad positions"]
        M3["Set 0 probability for first n tokens"]
        M4["mask = bernoulli(probability_matrix)"]
        M5["masked_expressions = expressions.masked_fill(mask, mask_value)"]
        
        M1 --> M2 --> M3 --> M4 --> M5
    end
    
    SampleMask -.-> "Masking Process"
```

**Expression Masking Process**

Sources: [scgpt/data_collator.py:115-132]()

## Handling Variable-Length Sequences

The `DataCollator` handles sequences of variable length through three main strategies:

1. **Padding**: For sequences shorter than the maximum length
2. **Truncation**: Simply cutting off sequences that are too long
3. **Sampling**: Randomly selecting a subset of positions from sequences that are too long (default behavior)

When sampling, the first `keep_first_n_tokens` positions are preserved, which is useful for keeping special tokens like CLS or batch labels.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Check{"Length == max_length?"}
    Check -->|"Yes"| Return["Return as is"]
    Check -->|"No"| TooLong{"Length > max_length?"}
    TooLong -->|"Yes"| SampleOrTrunc{"Sampling enabled?"}
    SampleOrTrunc -->|"Yes"| Sample["Random sample positions\n(keeping first n tokens)"]
    SampleOrTrunc -->|"No"| Truncate["Truncate to max_length"]
    TooLong -->|"No"| Pad["Pad to max_length"]
    
    Sample --> Return
    Truncate --> Return
    Pad --> Return
```

**Sequence Length Handling Logic**

Sources: [scgpt/data_collator.py:134-202]()

## Input and Output Data Format

The `DataCollator` expects input examples in a specific format and produces a standardized output format for the model:

### Input Format
Each example is a dictionary containing:
- `genes`: A tensor of gene IDs
- `expressions`: A tensor of expression values

### Output Format
The collated batch is a dictionary containing:
- `gene`: Padded gene ID tensors
- `expr`: Padded expression value tensors
- `masked_expr`: Expression values with some positions masked

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Input["Input Examples:\n- genes: Tensor\n- expressions: Tensor"] --> DataCollator["DataCollator.__call__()"]
    DataCollator --> Output["Output Batch:\n- gene: Tensor\n- expr: Tensor\n- masked_expr: Tensor"]
```

**Data Format Transformation**

Sources: [scgpt/data_collator.py:64-113]()

## Integration with the Overall System

The data processing pipeline is a crucial bridge between raw single-cell data and the scGPT transformer model. It prepares data in a format that allows the model to learn meaningful representations of gene expression patterns.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Data Processing Pipeline"
        Preprocess["Preprocessing"]
        GeneVocab["GeneVocab/Tokenizer"]
        DataCol["DataCollator"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Data Sources"
        Raw["Raw Gene Expression Data"]
        AnnData["AnnData Objects"]
        H5AD["H5AD Files"]
        CSV["CSV Files"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Model Components"
        Model["TransformerModel"]
        Training["Training System"]
    end
    
    Raw --> Preprocess
    AnnData --> Preprocess
    H5AD --> Preprocess
    CSV --> Preprocess
    
    Preprocess --> GeneVocab
    GeneVocab --> DataCol
    DataCol --> Model
    Model --> Training
```

**Data Processing in System Context**

Sources: [README.md:12-70](), [scgpt/data_collator.py:10-202]()

## Summary

The data processing pipeline in scGPT transforms raw gene expression data into a format suitable for transformer-based modeling through:

1. Preprocessing of gene expression data (filtering, normalization, log transformation, HVG selection)
2. Binning of continuous expression values
3. Tokenization of genes
4. Collation of data with padding, masking, and length standardization

This pipeline enables scGPT to effectively learn from single-cell RNA-seq data and perform various downstream tasks such as cell type annotation, dataset integration, perturbation prediction, and reference mapping.

# Page: Training Infrastructure

# Training System

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [scgpt/trainer.py](scgpt/trainer.py)

</details>



This document provides a technical overview of the training infrastructure in scGPT, explaining the core components responsible for training, evaluation, and testing workflows. For information about model architecture, see [Model Architecture](#2.1), and for data processing before training, see [Data Processing](#2.2).

## Overview

The scGPT training system consists of several core components designed to facilitate model training across different tasks including cell type annotation, dataset integration, perturbation prediction, and multi-omics analysis. The system handles the entire workflow from data preparation through training loops, evaluation, and performance reporting.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Data Preparation"
        prepData["prepare_data()"] --> tokenizedData["Tokenized Data"]
        tokenizedData --> prepDataloader["prepare_dataloader()"]
        prepDataloader --> DataLoader["PyTorch DataLoaders"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Training Loop"
        DataLoader --> trainFunc["train()"]
        trainFunc --> Optimizer["Optimizer Updates"]
        Optimizer --> Model["TransformerModel"]
        Model --> Loss["Loss Calculation"]
        Loss --> Optimizer
    end
    
    subgraph "Evaluation"
        DataLoader --> evalFunc["evaluate()"]
        evalFunc --> valMetrics["Validation Metrics"]
        DataLoader --> testFunc["test()"]
        testFunc --> testMetrics["Test Metrics"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Monitoring"
        trainFunc --> WandB["Weights & Biases"]
        evalFunc --> WandB
        testFunc --> WandB
    end
```

Sources: [scgpt/trainer.py:1-686]()

## Data Preparation for Training

Before training, data must be prepared with proper tokenization, masking, and batching. This preparation flow is crucial for the model to effectively learn from the data.

### Masked Value Preparation

A key part of scGPT's training approach is random masking of gene expression values, which allows the model to learn to predict these values:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Masking Process"
        input["Input Gene Expression Data"] --> tokenize["tokenize_and_pad_batch()"]
        tokenize --> tokens["Tokenized Gene Values"]
        tokens --> mask["random_mask_value()"]
        mask --> masked["Masked Values"]
        masked --> ready["Training-Ready Data"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Masked Data Structure"
        GeneIDs["Gene IDs"]
        Values["Masked Values"]
        TargetValues["Target Values"]
        BatchLabels["Batch Labels"]
        CelltypeLabels["Celltype Labels (optional)"]
        ModTypes["Modality Types (optional)"]
    end
```

Sources: [scgpt/trainer.py:24-115]()

### Data Loaders

The `prepare_dataloader` function creates PyTorch DataLoaders with support for batch-aware sampling, which is important for tasks involving multiple batches or domains:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    data["Training Data Dict"] --> SeqDataset["SeqDataset Class"]
    SeqDataset --> checkSample{"per_seq_batch_sample?"}
    checkSample -->|"Yes"| subsetSampler["SubsetsBatchSampler"]
    checkSample -->|"No"| standardLoader["Standard DataLoader"]
    subsetSampler --> finalLoader["Batch-Aware DataLoader"]
    standardLoader --> regularLoader["Regular DataLoader"]
```

Sources: [scgpt/trainer.py:118-170]()

## Training Process

The training process orchestrates the model training cycle, including forward passes, loss calculation, gradient computation and optimization steps.

### Training Loop

The `train` function in [scgpt/trainer.py:173-371]() handles the training loop for a single epoch:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    startTrain["Start Training Epoch"] --> iterateLoader["Iterate Through DataLoader"]
    iterateLoader --> forwardPass["Forward Pass through Model"]
    forwardPass --> computeLoss["Compute Loss Components"]
    computeLoss --> backprop["Gradient Calculation & Backpropagation"]
    backprop --> gradClip["Gradient Clipping"]
    gradClip --> optimStep["Optimizer Step"]
    optimStep --> scaleUpdate["Scaler Update (if AMP enabled)"]
    scaleUpdate --> logMetrics["Log Metrics"]
    logMetrics --> nextBatch{"More Batches?"}
    nextBatch -->|"Yes"| iterateLoader
    nextBatch -->|"No"| endEpoch["End Training Epoch"]
```

Sources: [scgpt/trainer.py:173-371]()

### Loss Components

The training system supports multiple loss components depending on the configured training objectives:

| Loss Component | Description | Configuration Flag |
|----------------|-------------|-------------------|
| GEP (Gene Expression Prediction) | MSE loss for masked gene values prediction | `config.GEP` |
| GEPC/MVC (Masked Value Prediction) | Secondary prediction task for cell embedding | `config.GEPC` |
| CLS (Classification) | Cell type classification loss | `config.CLS` |
| ECS (Elastic Cell Similarity) | Cell similarity constraint | `config.ESC` |
| DAB/DAR (Domain Adversarial) | Batch/domain adversarial loss | `config.DAR` |
| Zero-log probability | Bernoulli loss for explicit zero modeling | `config.explicit_zero_prob` |

Sources: [scgpt/trainer.py:235-289](), [examples/finetune_integration.py:466-497]()

### Optimization and Scaling

The training system uses:
- Adam optimizer with configurable learning rate
- Learning rate scheduling
- Gradient clipping for stability
- Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP) for faster training with lower memory usage

Sources: [scgpt/trainer.py:295-309](), [examples/finetune_integration.py:431-435]()

## Evaluation and Testing

The evaluation system provides mechanisms to assess model performance on validation and test data.

### Validation Process

The `evaluate` function computes validation metrics without updating model parameters:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    validData["Validation Data"] --> evalLoader["Evaluation DataLoader"]
    evalLoader --> modelEval["Model.eval()"]
    modelEval --> noGrad["torch.no_grad() Context"]
    noGrad --> forwardPass["Forward Pass"]
    forwardPass --> calcLoss["Calculate Loss"]
    calcLoss --> calcMetrics["Calculate Metrics"]
    calcMetrics --> logResults["Log Results"]
```

Sources: [scgpt/trainer.py:379-461]()

### Test Process and Metrics

For final evaluation on test data, the system provides:

1. The `test` function for classification tasks, calculating:
   - Accuracy, Precision, Recall
   - Macro and Micro F1 scores

2. The `eval_testdata` function for integration tasks, calculating:
   - scIB metrics for batch integration quality
   - UMAP visualizations of embeddings

Sources: [scgpt/trainer.py:507-686]()

## Configuration and Training Tasks

The scGPT training system is highly configurable to support different training tasks:

| Task | Description | Configuration |
|------|-------------|--------------|
| Annotation | Cell type annotation/classification | `config.task = "annotation"` |
| Integration | Dataset integration across batches | `config.task = "integration"` |
| Perturbation | Cellular perturbation prediction | `config.task = "perturb"` |
| Multi-omics | Integration of multiple omics data types | `config.task = "multiomic"` |

Each task utilizes different combinations of the loss functions and training objectives.

Sources: [scgpt/trainer.py:35](), [examples/finetune_integration.py:49-73]()

## Training Workflow

The complete training workflow combines these components into a coordinated process:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    startTraining["Start Training"] --> loadData["Load & Preprocess Data"]
    loadData --> prepareModel["Initialize/Load Model"]
    prepareModel --> beginLoop["Begin Training Loop"]
    
    subgraph "Per Epoch"
        beginLoop --> prepareDataEpoch["Prepare Data for Epoch"]
        prepareDataEpoch --> createLoaders["Create DataLoaders"]
        createLoaders --> trainEpoch["Train for One Epoch"]
        trainEpoch --> evaluate["Evaluate on Validation Set"]
        evaluate --> checkBest{"Best Model?"}
        checkBest -->|"Yes"| saveModel["Save Best Model"]
        checkBest -->|"No"| checkInterval{"Save Interval?"}
        saveModel --> checkInterval
        checkInterval -->|"Yes"| evalTest["Evaluate on Test Data"]
        checkInterval -->|"No"| updateLR["Update Learning Rate"]
        evalTest --> updateLR
        updateLR --> nextEpoch{"More Epochs?"}
        nextEpoch -->|"Yes"| prepareDataEpoch
        nextEpoch -->|"No"| endTraining["End Training"]
    end
```

Sources: [examples/finetune_integration.py:708-780]()

## Fine-tuning Existing Models

The system supports fine-tuning pretrained models for specific tasks:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    pretrainedModel["Pretrained Model"] --> loadWeights["Load Model Weights"]
    loadWeights --> compatCheck["Check Compatibility"]
    compatCheck -->|"Fully Compatible"| loadAll["Load All Parameters"]
    compatCheck -->|"Partially Compatible"| loadPartial["Load Matching Parameters"]
    loadAll --> continueTraining["Continue Training"]
    loadPartial --> continueTraining
```

Sources: [examples/finetune_integration.py:406-422]()

## Monitoring and Visualization

The training system integrates with Weights & Biases (wandb) for experiment tracking:

1. Defining metrics for tracking:
   ```python
   wandb.define_metric("valid/loss", summary="min", step_metric="epoch")
   wandb.define_metric("test/avg_bio", summary="max")
   ```

2. Logging training metrics per batch:
   ```python
   wandb.log(metrics_to_log)  # Log loss components
   ```

3. Visualization outputs:
   - UMAP plots for batch effect assessment
   - UMAP plots for cell type visualization
   - Training and validation curves

Sources: [scgpt/trainer.py:372-378](), [examples/finetune_integration.py:550-556](), [examples/finetune_integration.py:767-778]()

## Usage Example

A typical training workflow follows these steps:

1. Configure training settings (batch size, learning rate, etc.)
2. Prepare and tokenize data
3. Initialize the model or load a pretrained model
4. Create optimizer and scheduler
5. Run the training loop for specified epochs
6. Evaluate and save the best performing model
7. Generate and visualize results

For a complete example, see the `finetune_integration.py` script in the examples directory.

Sources: [examples/finetune_integration.py:1-797]()

# Page: Zero-Shot Applications

# Zero-Shot Applications

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)
- [scgpt/data_collator.py](scgpt/data_collator.py)
- [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb](tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb)
- [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration_Continual_Pretraining.ipynb](tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration_Continual_Pretraining.ipynb)
- [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Reference_Mapping.ipynb](tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Reference_Mapping.ipynb)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This page documents scGPT's zero-shot inference capabilities, which enable direct application of pretrained models to new single-cell RNA-seq datasets without any fine-tuning. Zero-shot applications represent scGPT's highest-impact feature cluster (importance: 34.40) and are designed for rapid deployment on novel datasets.

The two primary zero-shot tasks are:
- **Reference Mapping**: Transferring cell type annotations from reference to query datasets
- **Data Integration**: Batch correction and harmonization across multiple datasets

For information about fine-tuning scGPT for specific downstream tasks, see [Fine-tuning Applications](#6).

**Sources**: [README.md:16-20](), [High-Level Architecture Diagrams]()

## Overview

Zero-shot applications leverage scGPT's learned representations to perform downstream tasks without additional training. The core principle is that pretrained models encode biologically meaningful cell embeddings that can be directly used for similarity-based analysis, integration, and annotation transfer.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Input"
        RawData["Raw scRNA-seq Data<br/>(AnnData format)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Preprocessing"
        Preproc["Data Preprocessing<br/>HVG selection, normalization"]
        Binning["Expression Binning<br/>n_bins=51"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Pretrained Models"
        WholeHuman["scGPT_human<br/>33M cells, 60,697 genes"]
        CP["scGPT_CP<br/>Continual pretrained"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Embedding Generation"
        EmbedFunc["embed_data()<br/>scgpt.tasks.cell_emb"]
        CellEmb["Cell Embeddings<br/>adata.obsm['X_scGPT']"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Zero-Shot Tasks"
        RefMap["Reference Mapping<br/>FAISS k-NN search"]
        Integration["Data Integration<br/>scib metrics evaluation"]
    end
    
    RawData --> Preproc
    Preproc --> Binning
    Binning --> EmbedFunc
    WholeHuman --> EmbedFunc
    CP --> EmbedFunc
    EmbedFunc --> CellEmb
    CellEmb --> RefMap
    CellEmb --> Integration
```

**Diagram**: Zero-Shot Application Workflow

The workflow consists of three stages:
1. **Data Preparation**: Preprocessing raw counts, selecting highly variable genes (HVGs), and binning expression values
2. **Embedding Generation**: Forward pass through pretrained model to extract cell-level representations
3. **Task Execution**: Using embeddings for similarity search (reference mapping) or batch correction (integration)

**Sources**: [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Reference_Mapping.ipynb:23-36](), [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb:28-32]()

## Reference Mapping

Reference mapping transfers cell type annotations from a labeled reference dataset to an unlabeled query dataset by computing similarity in the embedding space. This enables rapid cell type identification without training a classifier.

### Workflow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant RefData as Reference Dataset
    participant QueryData as Query Dataset
    participant EmbedFunc as embed_data()
    participant FAISS as FAISS Index
    participant Output as Predicted Labels
    
    User->>RefData: Load with cell type labels
    User->>QueryData: Load without labels
    
    RefData->>EmbedFunc: Generate embeddings
    EmbedFunc-->>RefData: adata.obsm['X_scGPT']
    
    QueryData->>EmbedFunc: Generate embeddings
    EmbedFunc-->>QueryData: adata.obsm['X_scGPT']
    
    RefData->>FAISS: Build index from embeddings
    QueryData->>FAISS: Query k-NN (k neighbors)
    FAISS-->>Output: Return neighbor indices
    Output->>User: Transfer labels (mode voting)
```

**Diagram**: Reference Mapping Sequence

### Implementation Details

The reference mapping process involves:

1. **Embedding Generation**: Both reference and query datasets are processed through `embed_data()` to generate cell embeddings
2. **FAISS Indexing**: The reference embeddings are indexed using FAISS for efficient similarity search
3. **k-NN Search**: Query embeddings are compared against the index to find the k nearest reference cells
4. **Label Transfer**: Cell type labels are transferred using majority voting among the k neighbors

**Key Parameters**:
- `k`: Number of nearest neighbors (typically 5-15)
- `batch_size`: Embedding batch size (default: 64)
- `gene_col`: Column name for gene identifiers in AnnData.var

**Performance**: With FAISS GPU acceleration, similarity search takes <1 second for 10,000 query cells against 33+ million reference cells with <1GB memory footprint.

**Sources**: [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Reference_Mapping.ipynb:14-34](), [README.md:20]()

### Example Usage

The typical reference mapping workflow (from tutorial):

```python
# Load datasets
ref_adata = sc.read_h5ad('reference.h5ad')  # Has cell type labels
query_adata = sc.read_h5ad('query.h5ad')   # Missing labels

# Generate embeddings
ref_embed = scg.tasks.embed_data(
    ref_adata,
    model_dir,
    gene_col="gene_name",
    batch_size=64
)

query_embed = scg.tasks.embed_data(
    query_adata,
    model_dir,
    gene_col="gene_name",
    batch_size=64
)

# Build FAISS index and search
# (FAISS operations shown in tutorial)
```

The embeddings are stored in `adata.obsm['X_scGPT']` and can be used with any similarity search library.

**Sources**: [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Reference_Mapping.ipynb:191-233]()

## Data Integration

Data integration uses scGPT embeddings to harmonize multiple batches or datasets by removing technical variation while preserving biological signal. The embeddings naturally account for batch effects learned during pretraining.

### Evaluation Metrics

Integration quality is assessed using the scib (single-cell integration benchmarking) framework, which computes:

- **avgBIO**: Average of biological conservation metrics
  - NMI (Normalized Mutual Information) cluster/label
  - ARI (Adjusted Rand Index) cluster/label  
  - ASW (Average Silhouette Width) label
  
- **avgBATCH**: Average of batch mixing metrics
  - Graph connectivity
  - ASW label/batch

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Input Datasets"
        Batch1["Batch 1<br/>(e.g., 10X)"]
        Batch2["Batch 2<br/>(e.g., Smart-seq2)"]
        BatchN["Batch N<br/>(e.g., Drop-seq)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Embedding"
        Embed["embed_data()<br/>Per-batch processing"]
        Combined["Combined Embeddings<br/>adata.obsm['X_scGPT']"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Evaluation"
        UMAP["UMAP Visualization<br/>Check mixing"]
        ScibMetrics["scib.metrics.metrics()<br/>avgBIO + avgBATCH"]
        Clustering["Leiden Clustering<br/>For NMI/ARI"]
    end
    
    Batch1 --> Embed
    Batch2 --> Embed
    BatchN --> Embed
    Embed --> Combined
    Combined --> UMAP
    Combined --> Clustering
    Combined --> ScibMetrics
```

**Diagram**: Data Integration Evaluation Pipeline

### Implementation

The integration workflow:

1. **Preprocessing**: Each batch is preprocessed independently with HVG selection
2. **Embedding**: `embed_data()` generates embeddings preserving batch identities in metadata
3. **Concatenation**: Batch embeddings are combined into single AnnData object
4. **Evaluation**: scib metrics computed on combined embeddings

**Key Configuration**:
- `batch_key`: AnnData.obs column identifying batches
- `cell_type_key`: AnnData.obs column with cell type labels (for avgBIO)
- `embed_key`: Key in AnnData.obsm for embeddings (default: "X_scGPT")

**Sources**: [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb:141-189](), [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb:323-351]()

### Evaluation Function

The scib evaluation function from the tutorials:

```python
def scib_eval(adata, batch_key, cell_type_key, embed_key):
    results = scib.metrics.metrics(
        adata,
        adata_int=adata,
        batch_key=batch_key,
        label_key=cell_type_key,
        embed=embed_key,
        isolated_labels_asw_=False,
        silhouette_=True,
        hvg_score_=False,
        graph_conn_=True,
        pcr_=True,
        nmi_=True,
        ari_=True,
        # ... other metrics
    )
    
    result_dict["avg_bio"] = np.mean([
        result_dict["NMI_cluster/label"],
        result_dict["ARI_cluster/label"],
        result_dict["ASW_label"],
    ])
    
    result_dict["avg_batch"] = np.mean([
        result_dict["graph_conn"],
        result_dict["ASW_label/batch"],
    ])
    
    return result_dict
```

Higher avgBIO indicates better biological signal preservation, while higher avgBATCH indicates better batch mixing.

**Sources**: [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb:141-189]()

## Continual Pre-training Model (scGPT_CP)

The `scGPT_CP` model is a specialized variant designed for improved zero-shot performance on datasets with observable batch effects. It builds upon the whole-human pretrained model with additional supervised training.

### Architecture and Training

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Base Model"
        WholeHuman["scGPT_human<br/>Pretrained on 33M cells"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Continual Pretraining"
        TabulaSapiens["Tabula Sapiens Dataset<br/>Cell type supervision"]
        CPTraining["Continual Pretraining<br/>Cell type classification objective"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Model"
        CP["scGPT_CP Model<br/>Enhanced for batch-aware tasks"]
    end
    
    WholeHuman -->|Initialize weights| CPTraining
    TabulaSapiens -->|Provide labels| CPTraining
    CPTraining --> CP
    
    subgraph "Use Cases"
        BatchEffect["Datasets with<br/>technical batch effects"]
        Integration["Zero-shot integration"]
        Embedding["Cell embedding tasks"]
    end
    
    CP --> BatchEffect
    CP --> Integration
    CP --> Embedding
```

**Diagram**: scGPT_CP Model Development

### Key Differences

| Aspect | scGPT_human | scGPT_CP |
|--------|-------------|----------|
| **Training objective** | Masked gene prediction only | Masked prediction + cell type classification |
| **Supervision** | Self-supervised only | Self-supervised + supervised |
| **Training data** | 33M normal human cells | scGPT_human + Tabula Sapiens |
| **Vocabulary size** | 60,697 genes | 60,697 genes (same) |
| **Best for** | General-purpose tasks | Batch correction, integration |
| **Zero-shot performance** | Excellent baseline | Superior on datasets with batch effects |

### When to Use scGPT_CP

Use `scGPT_CP` for:
- **Data integration** tasks where batch effects are prominent
- **Reference mapping** when reference and query have different technical protocols
- **Cell embedding** tasks where batch-invariant representations are critical

Use `scGPT_human` for:
- General-purpose applications without severe batch effects
- Tasks requiring maximum generalization
- Applications where cell type supervision might introduce bias

**Sources**: [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration_Continual_Pretraining.ipynb:14-20](), [README.md:63]()

### Model Selection Example

From the Pancreas dataset tutorial using scGPT_CP:

```python
# For dataset with multiple technical batches
model_dir = Path("../../save/scGPT_CP")

# Generate embeddings with continual pretrained model
embed_adata = scg.tasks.embed_data(
    adata,
    model_dir,  # Uses scGPT_CP
    gene_col="Gene Symbol",
    batch_size=64,
)
```

The tutorial demonstrates that scGPT_CP achieves better avgBIO and avgBATCH scores on the Pancreas dataset which contains multiple technical batches (10X, Smart-seq2, etc.).

**Sources**: [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration_Continual_Pretraining.ipynb:115-351]()

## Cell Embedding Generation

The `embed_data()` function is the core interface for zero-shot applications. It performs a forward pass through the pretrained model to extract cell-level representations.

### Function Interface

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Inputs"
        AnnData["AnnData object<br/>Raw or preprocessed counts"]
        ModelDir["model_dir<br/>Path to checkpoint folder"]
        Config["Configuration<br/>gene_col, batch_size, etc."]
    end
    
    subgraph "embed_data() Function"
        VocabLoad["Load Vocabulary<br/>vocab.json"]
        ModelLoad["Load Pretrained Model<br/>best_model.pt"]
        GeneMatch["Match Genes to Vocab<br/>Handle missing genes"]
        Collate["DataCollator<br/>Padding, binning"]
        Forward["Forward Pass<br/>Extract cell embeddings"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output"
        EmbedAnnData["AnnData object<br/>With obsm['X_scGPT']"]
        Logging["Console logging<br/>Gene matching stats"]
    end
    
    AnnData --> VocabLoad
    ModelDir --> VocabLoad
    ModelDir --> ModelLoad
    Config --> Collate
    
    VocabLoad --> GeneMatch
    GeneMatch --> Collate
    ModelLoad --> Forward
    Collate --> Forward
    Forward --> EmbedAnnData
    GeneMatch --> Logging
```

**Diagram**: embed_data() Function Workflow

### Key Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description | Default |
|-----------|------|-------------|---------|
| `adata` | AnnData | Input single-cell dataset | Required |
| `model_dir` | Path/str | Directory containing model checkpoint and vocab | Required |
| `gene_col` | str | Column name in adata.var for gene names | "gene_name" |
| `batch_size` | int | Number of cells per forward pass batch | 64 |
| `return_new_adata` | bool | Return new AnnData vs modify in-place | True |
| `obs_to_save` | List[str] | Metadata columns to preserve | None |

### Gene Vocabulary Matching

The function automatically handles gene vocabulary matching:

1. **Load vocabulary**: Reads `vocab.json` from model checkpoint directory
2. **Match genes**: Maps genes in `adata.var[gene_col]` to vocabulary indices
3. **Handle mismatches**: Genes not in vocabulary are assigned index -1 and ignored
4. **Log statistics**: Reports matching success rate (e.g., "match 2978/3000 genes in vocabulary of size 60697")

**Sources**: [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Reference_Mapping.ipynb:191-196](), [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb:323-330]()

### Data Processing Pipeline

Before embedding generation, data undergoes preprocessing:

```mermaid
graph LR
    RawCounts["Raw Expression<br/>Counts"]
    Normalize["Normalization<br/>target_sum=1e4"]
    Log["Log Transform<br/>log1p"]
    HVG["HVG Selection<br/>n_top_genes"]
    Binning["Expression Binning<br/>51 bins"]
    Padding["Padding/Truncation<br/>max_length"]
    
    RawCounts --> Normalize
    Normalize --> Log
    Log --> HVG
    HVG --> Binning
    Binning --> Padding
    Padding --> Forward["Forward Pass<br/>Extract embeddings"]
```

**Diagram**: Data Preprocessing for Embedding Generation

The `DataCollator` class handles binning, padding, and truncation:
- **Binning**: Converts continuous expression values to discrete bins (n_bins=51)
- **Padding**: Pads sequences to max_length with pad_token_id
- **Truncation/Sampling**: Handles sequences exceeding max_length

**Sources**: [scgpt/data_collator.py:11-202](), [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb:276-300]()

### Output Format

The function returns an AnnData object with:
- **Original data**: Preserved from input (unless return_new_adata=False)
- **Embeddings**: Added to `adata.obsm['X_scGPT']` as numpy array of shape (n_cells, embedding_dim)
- **Metadata**: Selected obs columns preserved if specified

Example embedding extraction:

```python
# After running embed_data()
embeddings = embed_adata.obsm['X_scGPT']  # Shape: (n_cells, 512)

# Embeddings can be used for downstream tasks:
# - FAISS indexing for similarity search
# - UMAP/t-SNE visualization
# - Clustering (Leiden, Louvain)
# - Input to classifiers
```

**Sources**: [tutorials/zero-shot/Tutorial_ZeroShot_Integration.ipynb:323-351]()

## Pretrained Model Zoo

scGPT provides multiple pretrained models optimized for different use cases:

| Model Name | Description | Training Data | Use Cases | Download |
|------------|-------------|---------------|-----------|----------|
| **scGPT_human (whole-human)** | General-purpose model | 33M normal human cells | Default choice for most tasks | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1oWh_-ZRdhtoGQ2Fw24HP41FgLoomVo-y) |
| **scGPT_CP (continual pretrained)** | Batch-aware model | scGPT_human + Tabula Sapiens | Zero-shot integration, batch correction | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1_GROJTzXiAV8HB4imruOTk6PEGuNOcgB) |
| **brain** | Brain-specific | 13.2M brain cells | Brain tissue applications | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1vf1ijfQSk7rGdDGpBntR5bi5g6gNt-Gx) |
| **blood** | Blood-specific | 10.3M blood/bone marrow cells | Hematology applications | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1kkug5C7NjvXIwQGGaGoqXTk_Lb_pDrBU) |
| **heart** | Heart-specific | 1.8M heart cells | Cardiac applications | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1GcgXrd7apn6y4Ze_iSCncskX3UsWPY2r) |
| **lung** | Lung-specific | 2.1M lung cells | Respiratory applications | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/16A1DJ30PT6bodt4bWLa4hpS7gbWZQFBG) |
| **kidney** | Kidney-specific | 814K kidney cells | Renal applications | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1S-1AR65DF120kNFpEbWCvRHPhpkGK3kK) |
| **pan-cancer** | Cancer model | 5.7M cancer cells | Oncology applications | [Google Drive](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/13QzLHilYUd0v3HTwa_9n4G4yEF-hdkqa) |

### Model Selection Guidelines

```mermaid
graph TD
    Start{Task Type?}
    Start -->|General zero-shot| CheckBatch{Batch effects?}
    Start -->|Organ-specific| Organ[Use organ-specific model]
    Start -->|Cancer data| Cancer[Use pan-cancer model]
    
    CheckBatch -->|Minimal| WholeHuman[scGPT_human]
    CheckBatch -->|Significant| CP[scGPT_CP]
    
    Organ --> Brain[brain: 13.2M cells]
    Organ --> Blood[blood: 10.3M cells]
    Organ --> Heart[heart: 1.8M cells]
    Organ --> Lung[lung: 2.1M cells]
    Organ --> Kidney[kidney: 814K cells]
```

**Diagram**: Model Selection Decision Tree

**Recommendation**: Use `scGPT_human` as the default starting point. Switch to `scGPT_CP` if batch effects are a concern or if initial integration results show poor batch mixing. Organ-specific models may provide competitive or superior performance if your dataset closely matches their training data context.

**Sources**: [README.md:56-69]()
